note: Existing-source public educational gallery: CC photos and explicitly credited Bob Harms science/education-only photographs are distinguished. Source labels and arrows are not independent specimen voucher certification.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — THREE SPIKELETS PER NODE
tiles.details: Look at the physically archived compact green spike (panel 0) and real detached dry awned groups (panel 2). Actual head rows and long bristles are visible, but no existing image proves ONE intact rachis-node TRIAD: two lateral one-flowered reduced spikelets beside a central fertile one. The detached pictured groups (panels 1/2) lack preserved attachment to an erect rachis node. Photograph a still-attached mature node at 10–20× with a 1-mm ruler and separately trace each glume and lemma awn.
tiles.short: On a short erect bristly spike, magnify ONE rachis node: three one-flowered spikelets, not three florets.
tiles.status: REAL HEAD AND DETACHED AWNED GROUPS PHOTOGRAPHED; ATTACHED THREE-SPIKELET NODE STILL MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · ROOTED COOL-SEASON ANNUAL AND COLLAR
tiles.details: NEW exact-species source-authenticated Matt Lavin LOCALLY STORED CC BY-SA 2.0 panel 5 shows a green upper leaf sheath and emerging narrow blade on one actual plant. The overlapping sheath and stem can be taught without claiming any visible free ligule. Flora of North America and the Williamson County field treatment both describe an inner transparent membranous ligule only 0.2–0.8 mm long. A meaningful photo must open the INSIDE blade–sheath seam face-on, include a physical 1-mm scale, and separately show auricles absent or minute; outer sheath shoulders are NOT the free ligule. Neither panel 5 nor existing Montana patch (panel 3) shows the real fibrous annual root system. Photograph a legitimate collected live crown linked to the full head.
tiles.short: Now pictured: actual green leaf sheath, but inner ligule and roots remain missing
tiles.status: LOCAL EXACT-SPECIES LEAF/SHEATH PHOTO; FREE LIGULE AND ROOTED CROWN NOT PHOTOGRAPHED

tiles.heading: 03 · MEASURE THE FLOWERING SPIKE
tiles.details: The existing CC BY Montana head closeup (panel 0), newly archived attached green flowering spike (panel 6), and CC BY-SA 2.0 Montana flowering patch (panel 3) show erect, narrow, densely bristly little-barley spikes. FNA gives spike body around 2–9 cm by 3–7 mm before awns; actual existing images have no physical ruler and do not show a full rooted single plant. The true head is a terminal unbranched rachis bearing TRIADS at nodes, not a branched grass panicle. Record full spike length separately from bristle spread.
tiles.short: Usually erect spike 2–9 cm long and about 3–7 mm wide before the long bristles.
tiles.status: PUBLISHED SIZE — FULL SAME-PLANT SCALE NEEDED

tiles.heading: 04 · GLUMES, LEMMAS AND TWO AWN TYPES
tiles.details: The real source-labelled detached awned group photo in panel 2 shows long straight bristles, bundled pale glume/lemma-like bracts and pedicel-like stubs; it does NOT prove exactly which visible bract belongs to each original one-node central/lateral spikelet, and has no calibrated 1-mm ruler. The other archived macro panel 1 has a Git blob but its bytes still could not be independently retrieved for precise overlay review. For the crew, photograph a true attached full triad then detach the central and both laterals in order, showing straight glume awns versus the shorter fertile-lemma awn, with physical ruler. Keep existing published size ranges but do not claim them measured from these photos.
tiles.short: Central glumes 8–17 mm; central lemma body 5–8.5 mm; its awn 3.5–9.5 mm.

tiles.heading: 05 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: Foxtail barley H. jubatum (panel 4, DIFFERENT species) normally has much wider, more divergent plume-like awn-glumes and commonly a perennial rooted base. Little barley's true head in panel 0 is narrower and commonly erect; leaf sheath in new panel 5 helps establish vegetative context, not definite ligule identity. Introduced wall barley H. murinum often has conspicuous auricles and ciliate central glume margins; these require genuine 1-mm photo evidence. IMPORTANT: even within Hordeum, traits of auricles may vary; never identify by absence alone. Elymus wildryes have commonly paired MULTIFLORED spikelets rather than the barley triad of one-flowered units. Confirm rachis attachments first.
tiles.short: Foxtail barley has longer splayed glumes; wildryes have multiflowered spikelets; rye has one spikelet per node.
tiles.status: LOOK-ALIKE KEY — MATCHED NODE MACROS MISSING

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE AND PHOTO HANDOFF
tiles.details: SIX exact-species JPEG files are locally archived: the four earlier photos plus Matt Lavin's true exterior sheath (panel 5) and still-attached green spike closeup (panel 6). Three old photos had prior verified pixel readbacks; an older fourth JPEG is physically stored but its detailed pixel review remains pending. The two new archived photos have source/rights and decoded-image validation. SIX species-matched teaching panels now include credited CC BY-SA 2.0 LOCALLY ARCHIVED upper-sheath photo (panel 5) and intact green head closeup (panel 6); one other-species foxtail comparison is panel 4. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: one attached source-vouched Hays rooted annual from fibrous crown to full flowering head; one opened inner 0.2–0.8-mm ligule with physical 1-mm ruler; one mature intact rachis node with central fertile plus two reduced lateral spikelets; separate glume/lemma awn origins and measured size. NEEDS_SITE_QA: source CC BY on iNat photo, existing old panel 1 byte/pixel review, licensed creator notices, arrow alignment and actual rights-filtered Pages mobile display. Minnesota Wildflowers macro photos have special copyrighted reproduction restrictions; Go Botany prohibits direct hotlinking. Both may be linked as research PAGES, NOT copied or hotlinked photographs.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — additional licensed sheath photo, critical ligule/triad/root missing

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: Little barley (*Hordeum pusillum*) is an ANNUAL cool-season low tuft. In late winter/spring look for a short straight usually erect BRISTLY SPIKE; local physically archived close-up shows head shape, and Matt Lavin's new licensed group photo shows detached awned units. Now MAGNIFY ONE ATTACHED RACHIS NODE: BARLEYS have 3 associated ONE-flowered spikelets, central usually fertile and two lateral smaller/reduced, unlike paired MULTIFLOWERED Elymus wildryes. Little barley's mature glumes are relatively straight and short (FNA central glumes commonly 8–17 mm including awn). H. jubatum foxtail barley likewise has three per node but very long widely divergent glumes, broad often nodding head, perennial growth. Beware introduced wall barley H. murinum (fanlike groups and often well-developed auricles). Confirm glume margins and a small membranous ligule before species ID; do not use bristly silhouette alone.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Cool-season annual grass, loosely tufted and usually 10–60 cm tall. Native in Texas at state/ecoregion level; do not presume any fresh county-native certification from this visual enrichment.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Look at the physically archived compact green spike (panel 0) and real detached dry awned groups (panel 2). Actual head rows and long bristles are visible, but no existing image proves ONE intact rachis-node TRIAD: two lateral one-flowered reduced spikelets beside a central fertile one. The detached pictured groups (panels 1/2) lack preserved attachment to an erect rachis node. Photograph a still-attached mature node at 10–20× with a 1-mm ruler and separately trace each glume and lemma awn.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Short usually erect dense terminal spike; at each rachis node a triad of ONE-flowered spikelets, the central fertile and lateral companions commonly sterile. Closely packed bristle-like glumes make the little barley head appear bottlebrush-like.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Hordeum jubatum (foxtail barley; native broadly to much of North America, including Texas in Kew state-scale account; LOCAL Hays status unreviewed) is usually PERENNIAL, with long broadly outward-fanning awnlike glumes (up to 85 mm) and a fluffy/nodding spike. H. pusillum is ANNUAL, with short relatively erect spike, straighter glumes ~8–17 mm and shorter awns. BOTH species have ONE-FLOWERED spikelet TRIADS, central fertile/laterals mainly sterile; this is a GENUS trait. Elymus wildryes have more than one flower per spikelet and generally two/sometimes more spikelets per rachis node. Introduced H. murinum has broad fanlike glume groups and often auricles; planted H. vulgare has robust head/cultivar variability; rye Secale cereale differs in spikelet arrangement. Count a real node and inspect glumes, not merely head fuzz.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

The new arrow points to visible overlapping bracts, NOT a confidently isolated glume or lemma. The original central versus two lateral positions at an ATTACHED rachis node cannot be conclusively mapped from this detached view; no millimeter scale or local Hays voucher is provided.

panels.label: LITTLE BARLEY — many narrow upright ripe spikes in a grassy opening
panels.caption: This image shows a patch with several short dense little-barley seed spikes, upright and often pale or tan at maturity. Learn the narrow, rather stiff habit. It does NOT show an individual spikelet triad, correct collar, or isolated rooted annual. Photo from Montana, not Hays.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin

panels.caption: Real little-barley upper shoot with green outer leaf sheath surrounding the stalk and narrow blade extending at the junction. This photo is now STORED LOCALLY under the original CC BY-SA 2.0 license, not hotlinked. It does NOT resolve the inner free 0.2–0.8 mm ligule, authentic roots or auricles. Montana source, not Hays County.

panels.label: INTACT GREEN SPIKE — overlapping awned flowering units attached to the central axis
panels.caption: The green little-barley spike is intact, and narrow pointed flowering bracts and long awns overlap in close view. Follow the central upright stalk from base to tip, then compare detached pieces in earlier panels. The photograph does NOT isolate one complete 3-spikelet rachis node with a 1-mm scale, and individual glumes/lemmas should not be labeled from this view.

memory_rule: THREE one-flowered spikelets at ONE barley rachis node (center usually fertile, two laterals reduced) = Hordeum genus; it does not prove LITTLE species. Little: erect narrow annual head with straight/ascending short glumes; foxtail: much longer widely divergent awn-glumes plus usually perennial/nodding growth.
safety_note: 2026-10-27 reconciled live canonical inventory: 6 local exact-species image records, 7 gallery panels (6 little barley + 1 foxtail barley comparison), 8 existing markers reported by the photo lane. Panel 5 is LOCAL exterior sheath (not exposed true ligule); panel 6 is LOCAL attached green spike (not an isolated verified three-spikelet rachis node). Older panel 1 byte/pixel verification remains pending. Do not claim measured glumes, ligule, connected roots or website deployment.
field_rule: Genus: 3 ONE-FLOWERED spikelets on one barley rachis node. Species: little annual narrow erect spike + short straight glumes; foxtail = nodding feather with longer splayed glumes and perennial base. Detached awned group is NOT confirmation of the central fertile spikelet; get attached node macro.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.

morphology.habit: Cool-season annual grass, loosely tufted and usually 10–60 cm tall. Native in Texas at state/ecoregion level; do not presume any fresh county-native certification from this visual enrichment.
morphology.inflorescence: Short usually erect dense terminal spike; at each rachis node a triad of ONE-flowered spikelets, the central fertile and lateral companions commonly sterile. Closely packed bristle-like glumes make the little barley head appear bottlebrush-like.
morphology.spikelets: Central fertile floret with short lemma awn, surrounded at the node by two smaller sterile lateral spikelets. Glumes usually straight/upright ~8–17 mm (broad FNA range); the small fertile lemma ~5–8.5 mm, awn ~3.5–9.5 mm; exact dimensions require 1-mm macro.
